comments.name: Yann LeCun
comments.text:
"one economist Nobel laureate was wrong once about one thing, therefore all economists are wrong" is not good logic. 

The whole history of technological progress is one in which people became more productive and some professions were progressively displaced or eliminated. 
Yet this has never caused long-term mass unemployment. 
AI is just another one of those technological revolutions.
People like Dario present it as qualitatively different from previous revolutions.
It's not.

comments.name: Yann LeCun

@DrTonyCarden @Ph_Aghion @erikbryn No! 
It really doesn't differ qualitatively from previous technological revolutions. 
That's the whole point.

People like Dario present it as qualitatively different.
They are just deluded or biased by their vested interests in magnifying the impact of their work.

comments.name: Kleon
comments.text:
Hot take: the moat for solo AI builders isn't technical skill. It's the willingness to do the boring parts.

Anyone can spin up a Claude Code project. Few will spend 3 weeks debugging a browser automation edge case at 2am. Even fewer will cold-email 50 professors to validate a data product before writing a line of code.

The AI tools are converging — everyone has access to the same models. What separates builders who ship from builders who prototype is tolerance for tedium.

I've built 40+ automated skills. The impressive part isn't the architecture. It's that 80% of my time was spent on dedup logic, rate limit handling, and CSV parsing. The unglamorous 80% IS the product.

comments.name: Kleon
comments.text:
观察了一个月X上的高热帖，总结了4种最容易火的pattern：

1. 反直觉数据帖 — 给一个跟常识相反的数据点，比如"只有25%的AI项目有ROI"。数据越具体越好，来源越权威越好

2. 第一人称翻车帖 — "我做了X，结果发现Y"。关键是要有具体失败细节，不是泛泛的"创业很难"

3. 行业内幕帖 — "在X公司的时候发现..."。大厂出来的人讲内部真实情况，永远有人看

4. 框架总结帖 — 把一个复杂现象归纳成3-5个要点。List format天然适合手机阅读

90%的0互动帖子都是第5种：观点陈述帖 — "我觉得X很重要"。没有数据没有故事没有框架，只有一个opinion。opinion不值钱，experience才值钱。

comments.text:
The irony yevgenydevine highlights: Krugman’s 1998 quote predicted the internet would have only minor economic impact (like the fax machine). He meant it broadly, and he was wrong—the internet exploded qualitatively (new industries, communication, culture).

But in the specific quantitative sense you’re focused on (employment/labor market effects), his prediction *did* fully materialize: no mass unemployment, just job shifts and adaptation. Economists like those Yann cites argue tech revolutions don’t wipe out jobs net—they evolve the market. You’re citing Krugman to predict 99% AI unemployment, missing that parallel.

comments.name: Venkatesan Mahendran
comments.text:
You are right. In a capitalist world, everyone somehow ends up with a job. The real question is whether it is something you actually enjoy doing.

Also, the idea that half the jobs will disappear in a few years because of AI feels a bit dramatic. That is not really something technologists can confidently predict. Economists have been studying job cycles for decades, and even they do not throw around such neat, scary numbers.

I am not a full-on capitalism fan, but one thing it does well is expansion. Old jobs fade out, new ones show up. The titles change, the tools change… but we humans somehow always find new ways to stay busy and it's billable.
